sec.title: Chemo-curcumin nano-delivery systems
sec.p: Synergistic therapy utilizing nanoparticle co-delivery systems represents a pivotal advancement in enhancing curcumin’s anticancer efficacy by leveraging complementary mechanisms with conventional chemotherapeutics. This approach fundamentally addresses multiple limitations of traditional chemotherapy, including multidrug resistance (MDR), systemic toxicity, and inadequate tumor penetration [220]. The strategic co-encapsulation of curcumin with chemotherapeutic agents within nanocarriers creates multifunctional platforms that simultaneously overcome biological barriers while amplifying therapeutic outcomes through pharmacodynamic interactions.

Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles have emerged as particularly effective carriers due to their biocompatibility, controlled release properties, and adaptability for surface functionalization [221, 222]. In breast cancer models, doxorubicin-curcumin (CUR-DOX) nanoformulations demonstrate remarkable synergy by concurrently attacking cancer cells through multiple pathways. Specifically, Sarkar et al. reported that this combination treatment significantly induces S-phase cell cycle arrest in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) cells, achieving a 3-fold higher apoptosis rate compared to monotherapy, effectively halting proliferation in this aggressive subtype and demonstrating superior efficacy compared to monotherapies [223].

In the context of breast cancer MDR, recent investigations have elucidated that the synergistic potency of Curcumin and Doxorubicin (DOX) within polymeric nanocarriers (e.g., nanomicelles) extends beyond simple co-delivery [224]. To further refine this synergy, Zeng et al. developed a “Shell-Core” bilayer nanoparticle system as a co-delivery platform. This advanced architecture is engineered to render a synchronized response to the tumor microenvironment, thereby optimizing the spatiotemporal release of both drugs to maximize antitumor effects and overcome resistance [224]. Similarly, a 2023 study [225] demonstrated that nanomicelles co-encapsulating DOX and Curcumin could effectively reverse multidrug resistance in cancer cells by competitively inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux pump [226]. The nanoformulation achieved high encapsulation efficiency and facilitated the nuclear accumulation of DOX, which is typically expelled in resistant cells [227]. Furthermore, recent advancements have introduced targeted co-assembly micelles that exhibit synergistic cytotoxicity. These systems not only enhanced the intracellular retention of DOX compared to free drug combinations but also utilized Curcumin to modulate apoptotic signaling pathways, thereby significantly improving anti-tumor efficacy against resistant breast cancer cell lines. Advanced formulations incorporating photoresponsive elements, such as perfluorooctyl bromide (PFOB) in PLGA nanoparticles, enable laser-triggered drug release that further enhances intracellular doxorubicin accumulation by 76–84% [228], significantly suppressing tumor proliferation and migration through reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and caspase-3 activation. Targeted delivery systems like transferrin-conjugated nanoparticles demonstrate superior biodistribution, with recent evidence showing 40% greater tumor accumulation than non-targeted versions, substantially improving survival outcomes in xenograft models [229].

For pancreatic cancer, the co-delivery of gemcitabine and curcumin (GEM-CUR) in albumin-based nanoparticles addresses the critical challenge of stromal barrier penetration. The 2022 RGD-HSA-GEM/CUR nanoparticle system demonstrates a 200% improvement in drug diffusion through tumor stroma compared to free drug combinations [193]. This enhanced penetration translates to significant in vivo efficacy, with RGD-modified nanoparticles reducing tumor volumes to 354.6 mm³, representing a 55% reduction compared to the free drug group (781.4 mm³) and a 71% reduction compared to the saline control group after 27 days treatment, attributed to curcumin’s ability to downregulate fibrosis-associated proteins and inhibit cancer-associated fibroblasts. The targeted formulation simultaneously suppresses MDR1 and BCL-2 expression at mRNA levels, overcoming inherent chemoresistance while maintaining negligible systemic toxicity as evidenced by stable murine body weights throughout treatment [230].

Beyond direct cytotoxicity, emerging research highlights curcumin’s immunomodulatory synergy with checkpoint inhibitors. Nanodelivery systems enhance curcumin’s bioavailability sufficiently to inhibit STAT3 signaling in dendritic cells, thereby augmenting anti-PD-1 therapy by reducing regulatory T-cell infiltration and restoring CD8 + T-cell functionality [231, 232]. This immunotherapeutic combination demonstrates particular promise in resistant malignancies where conventional immunotherapy fails, though clinical validation remains ongoing. Similarly, innovative photothermal-curcumin hybrid systems like gold-nanorod vesicles enable sequential drug release under near-infrared irradiation, achieving synergistic cell cycle arrest (S-phase) and apoptosis induction unattainable with single-modality approaches [233].

Despite these advances, clinical translation requires optimization of drug loading capacities (currently averaging <10% w/w in polymeric systems), refinement of tumor-specific targeting ligands, and comprehensive toxicological profiling [222]. Future developments should focus on multifunctional “smart” nanoparticles responsive to tumor microenvironmental cues (pH, enzymes, redox gradients) to achieve spatiotemporal control over drug release [234]. The integration of stromal-modulating agents alongside cytotoxic combinations presents a promising frontier for overcoming physical barriers in desmoplastic tumors [230].

Collectively, these nano-enabled combination strategies transform curcumin from a pharmacologically challenged compound into a potent cornerstone of modern cancer therapy regimens. By simultaneously addressing bioavailability limitations, tumor microenvironment barriers, and multidrug resistance while amplifying therapeutic synergy, engineered co-delivery systems significantly expand the clinical potential of curcumin-based anticancer interventions.

sec.title: Immunotherapy combinations
sec.p: The integration of curcumin (CUR) with immune checkpoint inhibitors, particularly anti-PD-1 antibodies, represents a cutting-edge strategy in cancer immunotherapy by synergistically remodeling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Curcumin exerts multifaceted immunomodulatory effects, including inhibition of the STAT3 signaling pathway, which is frequently hyperactivated in tumors and contributes to dendritic cell (DC) dysfunction and T-cell exhaustion. By targeting STAT3, CUR restores DC-mediated antigen presentation and enhances the priming of tumor antigen-specific CD8 + T cells, thereby augmenting the efficacy of PD-1 blockade [231]. In preclinical studies using the 4T1 murine breast cancer model, the combination of CUR and anti-PD-1 therapy significantly increased intratumoral CD8 + T-cell infiltration by 50% while concurrently reducing regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), which collectively dismantle immunosuppressive barriers and potentiate cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity [235, 236]. This immunogenic shift is further amplified by CUR’s ability to repolarize tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from the pro-tumor M2 phenotype to the antitumor M1 phenotype and to suppress immunosuppressive cytokines like IL-10, TGF-β, and VEGF [237].

Despite its potent immunomodulatory properties, curcumin’s clinical translation has been hindered by poor aqueous solubility, rapid systemic metabolism, and low oral bioavailability (<1%). To overcome these limitations, smart nanoparticle delivery systems have been engineered to enhance CUR’s pharmacokinetics and tumor-targeted delivery. Liposomal formulations, for instance, encapsulate CUR within biocompatible phospholipid bilayers, shielding it from degradation and improving cellular uptake. Moreover, specific protein-based nanocarriers like heavy chain ferritin (HFn) nanocages (Cur@HFn) have demonstrated precise pH-triggered disassembly. These systems exhibit a 3-fold faster drug release rate at endosomal pH (5.0–6.0) compared to physiological pH, and have achieved approximately 50% tumor regression in breast cancer models by ensuring high intracellular drug concentration [238]. Surface modification with polyethylene glycol (PEG) extends circulation half-life, while functionalization with ligands (e.g., glycoproteins or antibodies) enables active targeting to tumor cells or immune cells within the TME [11]. Similarly, polymeric nanoparticles (e.g., PLGA-based carriers) and micellar systems (e.g., Pluronic/PCL copolymers) achieve high drug-loading capacities and sustained release, significantly boosting CUR concentrations in tumor tissues [239]. In the 4T1 model, nanoformulations like Gemini-CUR—a lipid-polymeric hybrid nanoparticle—demonstrated enhanced tumor accumulation and potentiated apoptosis through downregulation of MMP-9, VEGF, and Bcl-2, providing a robust platform for combination immunotherapy [240, 241].

Emerging clinical evidence supports the feasibility of CUR-based nanomedicines in augmenting immunotherapy. A pilot trial combining oral nanocurcumin with pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) in cervical and uterine cancer patients reported improved therapeutic responses and reduced immunosuppressive factors, suggesting gut microbiota modulation as a potential mechanism [242]. Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating nano-CUR formulations (e.g., liposomal CUR and micellar CUR) across diverse cancers, with several in Phase I/II. However, challenges persist, including batch-to-batch variability in nanocarrier synthesis, long-term biosafety concerns, and the need for optimized dosing regimens in combinatorial protocols [243]. Future directions include developing stimuli-responsive nanocarriers that release CUR in response to TME-specific cues (e.g., pH or enzymes) and hybrid nanoparticles co-delivering CUR with other immunomodulators (e.g., TLR agonists) to further amplify antitumor immunity [244].

In summary, CUR nanoparticle delivery systems not only resolve bioavailability limitations but also strategically reprogram the TME to overcome resistance to PD-1 blockade. As clinical trials advance, these targeted nanoplatforms hold transformative potential for enhancing the precision and efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.

sec.title: Theranostic applications
sec.p: The integration of iron oxide-curcumin hybrid nanoparticles represents a transformative advancement in theranostic oncology, leveraging multimodal imaging capabilities to achieve real-time tumor tracking and enhanced therapeutic efficacy. These nanoconstructs, synthesized via green co-precipitation or metal-chelated methods [245], exploit curcumin’s inherent bioactivity while incorporating superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast. The resulting hybrids exhibit synergistic functionalities: SPIONs provide high T₂-weighted MRI contrast for anatomical localization [246], while curcumin-derived fluorescence enables cellular-level visualization [247, 248]. In CT26 colorectal carcinoma models, such dual-labeled nanoparticles achieved 60% tumor suppression through mechanisms involving pH-responsive drug release and oxidative stress amplification [249]. This suppression is attributed to curcumin’s modulation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways and iron-mediated Fenton reactions, which collectively induce apoptosis and inhibit metastasis [250].

Recent innovations in surface engineering have further optimized tumor targeting and biocompatibility. Functionalization with polyethylene glycol (PEG) or tumor-homing peptides (e.g., RGD) extends systemic circulation while facilitating active accumulation in neoplastic tissues via enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects [251]. A study demonstrated that copper silicate nanoparticles co-loaded with curcumin could deplete intratumoral glutathione and alleviate hypoxia, thereby amplifying photodynamic-chemodynamic synergy and achieving 80% growth inhibition in CT26 models [252]. Such combinatorial approaches address the tumor microenvironment’s immunosuppressive nature, as evidenced by macrophage repolarization toward antitumor M1 phenotypes [253].

Beyond monotherapy, these platforms enable precision-guided synergistic regimens. MRI-fluorescence navigation permits spatially controlled hyperthermia or radiotherapy, where localized heating from alternating magnetic fields triggers curcumin release while sensitizing cancer cells to ionizing radiation [254, 255]. The 2023 DEGRO trial highlighted zinc oxide-curcumin hybrids enhancing radiotherapeutic efficacy through ROS potentiation and DNA damage amplification [256]. Moreover, carrier-free nanodrug assemblies (e.g., curcumin-siRNA conjugates) exploit endogenous biomolecules for self-delivery, bypassing traditional nanocarrier limitations [257].

Crucially, nanoparticle encapsulation overcomes curcumin’s pharmacokinetic barriers: poor aqueous solubility, rapid glucuronidation, and systemic clearance. Lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles (e.g., alginate/chitosan-coated SPIONs) enhance oral bioavailability by approximately 20-fold in rodent models via lymphatic uptake and enzymatic degradation shielding [258, 259]. The 2024 glucose oxidase-Fe₃O₄ system exemplifies metabolic modulation, where cascadic ROS generation from glucose depletion and curcumin release induces immunogenic cell death [250]. Future directions include CRISPR-Cas9 co-delivery for gene-editing-enhanced therapy and clinical translation of GMP-compliant nanoformulations [257].

Collectively, iron oxide-curcumin theranostics epitomize next-generation oncology tools, merging diagnosis, targeted delivery, and multimodal treatment within a unified platform. Their efficacy in aggressive models like CT26 colorectal cancer underscores potential clinical relevance, pending large-scale biocompatibility studies and Phase I trials [260].

sec.title: Clinical translation: from early failures to emerging successes
sec.p: The clinical translation of smart nanoparticle delivery systems for curcumin has evolved significantly over the past 5 years. While early phase I studies (e.g., the 2018 Lipocurc™ trial) [261] primarily identified dose-limiting toxicities and pharmacokinetic instability [236], recent investigations have shifted focus toward combinatorial regimens and biomarker-driven stratification, revealing more robust efficacy signals.

sec.title: Safety, pharmacokinetics, and formulation constraints
sec.p: Recent advancements have successfully addressed the historical challenge of negligible oral bioavailability. A pivotal 2023 crossover study demonstrated that a novel solvent-free co-grinding nanostrategy (CUMINUP60®) achieved a 178-fold increase in plasma Area Under the Curve (AUC) in healthy human volunteers compared to standard crystalline curcumin [79]. Unlike earlier formulations that precipitated rapidly, this strategy utilized water-soluble carriers to maintain supersaturation, significantly extending the absorption window without adverse events. Similarly, comparative pharmacokinetic evaluations in 2024 confirmed that optimized solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) and amphiphilic polymer assessments could extend the systemic circulation half-life from minutes to hours, effectively shielding the labile β-diketone moiety from hydrolytic degradation. Regarding safety profile updates, clinical data from nanomicellar formulations have demonstrated superior tolerability compared to the hemolytic risks observed in earlier liposomal infusions [24]. In a randomized trial involving COVID-19 patients (2021), nanomicellar curcumin (Sinacurcumin®) administered at 80 mg/day for 14 days showed no hepato-renal toxicity, with patients exhibiting stable serum creatinine and liver enzyme levels, thereby establishing a safety baseline for sustained oral dosing in inflammatory conditions [262]. However, formulation constraints persist in the realm of long-term biocompatibility. 2023–2024 toxicological reviews highlight that while acute toxicity is manageable, the chronic accumulation of non-biodegradable carriers (e.g., certain metallic or high-molecular-weight polymeric components) in the reticuloendothelial system remains a concern [10]. Furthermore, achieving consistent drug loading remains a bottleneck; recent comparisons indicate that while polymeric micelles offer high stability, they often suffer from low drug loading capacities (<10%), necessitating large carrier volumes to achieve therapeutic doses in oncology, which complicates patient compliance and industrial scalability.

sec.title: Efficacy endpoints and clinical outcomes
sec.p: Despite these constraints, preliminary efficacy signals have been observed. In the Lipocurc™ trial, while no objective response rate (ORR) was observed per RECIST v1.1, two heavily pretreated patients (one with prostate carcinoma and another with colon carcinoma) exhibited significant tumor marker reductions and transient clinical benefit, suggesting potential biological activity in select subpopulations. More encouraging efficacy data were derived from combinatorial regimens. Early-phase trials such as the CUFOX IIa and G-NLC + FOLFIRI studies have shown positive outcomes, including improved overall survival (OS) (HR = 0.339) and progression-free survival (PFS) (12.8 months) [172]. Regarding NanoCurc™, although it demonstrates robust preclinical promise by enhancing blood-brain barrier penetration in glioblastoma models [263], its clinical evaluation has often targeted non-oncological endpoints. For instance, ongoing studies (e.g., NCT04853199) prioritize inflammatory biomarkers in breast cancer over antitumor efficacy [264]. Consequently, the clinical translation of curcumin nanoformulations remains at an early stage, with findings derived from small, often non-randomized studies that require validation in larger, controlled trials [265].

sec.title: Limitations of current clinical evidence
sec.p: Current clinical findings, while promising, are constrained by inherent limitations in trial design and evidence quality.

sec.title: Sample size and study design
sec.p: Most efficacy data are derived from Phase I/II trials with small cohorts (e.g., N = 28 in CUFOX, N = 44 in G-NLC trials). The lack of large-scale, randomized, multicenter Phase III trials limits the statistical power to confirm survival benefits (OS) definitively.

sec.title: Patient heterogeneity
sec.p: Early-phase trials often enroll heavily pretreated patients with refractory disease, which may obscure the true efficacy of nanoformulations due to compromised immune systems or multidrug resistance. Future trials require better patient stratification based on biomarkers (e.g., FRα or CD44 expression) to identify responders.

sec.title: Endpoint interpretation
sec.p: Many studies rely on surrogate endpoints like Progression-Free Survival (PFS) or tumor marker reduction. While valuable, these do not always translate to long-term Overall Survival (OS) benefits, necessitating longer follow-up periods.

However, resolving these clinical trial limitations is only half the battle. Even if efficacy is proven, the widespread adoption of these nanomedicines is currently bottlenecked by upstream industrial challenges, specifically the difficulty of manufacturing these complex systems at a commercial scale (Table 4).Table 4

sec.title: Barriers to translation: the “bench-to-bedside” gap
sec.p: The clinical translation of smart nanoparticle delivery systems for curcumin faces substantial challenges in scalability and manufacturing, with batch variability and Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliance representing critical hurdles. PLGA nanoparticles (NPs), a widely studied carrier for curcumin, exhibit significant inter-batch heterogeneity in encapsulation efficiency (EE), with reported fluctuations ranging from 21% to 94% [266]. This inconsistency primarily stems from subtle variations in solvent selection, stabilizer concentrations (e.g., PVA, vitamin E-TPGS), emulsification methods (single vs. double emulsion), and even operator technique, as demonstrated by studies showing trained individuals producing NPs with average diameters varying between 220 nm and 364 nm despite identical protocols [267]. Such variability directly impacts critical quality attributes (CQAs) like particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, and drug loading [268], ultimately compromising the reproducibility of pharmacokinetic profiles and therapeutic efficacy in vivo. For instance, ζ-potential measurements across different PLGA NP formulations can range from −31.1 mV to +3.71 mV [269], influencing colloidal stability and biodistribution, while PDI values from 0.192 to 0.542 indicate broad size distributions that affect tumor penetration and clearance rates. Ensuring batch-to-batch consistency necessitates rigorous process control, including meticulous characterization of each batch and strategic pooling strategies to homogenize critical parameters before further modification or administration [270].

The stringent requirements of GMP compliance introduce another layer of complexity and cost to nanoscale manufacturing. Establishing and maintaining the specialized infrastructure, cleanroom facilities, and analytical instrumentation required for reproducible, large-scale production under GMP conditions represents a significant financial barrier, with initial investments potentially reaching $5 million [271]. This high cost is compounded by the inherent complexity of nanomedicine manufacturing, which involves multiple unit operations (emulsification, purification, sterilization, lyophilization) and demands exquisite control over numerous critical process parameters (CPPs) to ensure consistent CQAs [272]. Even minor deviations in parameters like mixing intensity, solvent evaporation rate, or temperature during scale-up can drastically alter NP properties (size, EE, release kinetics) and, consequently, their biological fate and safety profile [273]. Furthermore, sterilization of thermolabile nanocarriers like liposomes or certain polymeric NPs without compromising stability remains a persistent challenge, often requiring expensive aseptic processing techniques instead of terminal heat sterilization [274, 275]. The analytical burden is also heightened, requiring multiple orthogonal characterization techniques (DLS, TEM, HPLC, etc.) for comprehensive batch release testing due to the multifaceted nature of NPs.

Addressing these scalability and manufacturing hurdles requires innovative engineering solutions and advanced process control strategies. Microfluidic technology has emerged as a promising approach to enhance batch consistency. Compared to traditional bulk nanoprecipitation, microfluidic platforms enable superior control over mixing dynamics, shear forces, and supersaturation levels, facilitating the production of NPs with significantly narrower size distributions (PDI < 0.15) and improved reproducibility [276]. For example, optimized microfluidic systems can generate homogeneous PLGA NPs (~150 nm) with high reproducibility, and surface modifications (e.g., with cell-penetrating peptides) can be performed predictably [277]. Scaling microfluidic production is achievable through strategies like parallelization of microchannels, flow rate optimization, and device engineering, with recent reports demonstrating production rates exceeding 1300 mg/h of PLGA NPs [278]. Continuous manufacturing platforms, integrating inline ultrasonication [279] or static mixers [280] with downstream purification like tangential flow filtration (TFF), offer advantages in process control, reduced footprint, and easier scale-up compared to batch processes, aligning better with GMP requirements [272]. TFF, in particular, has proven effective in removing residual solvents and concentrating NPs while maintaining critical attributes like size and PDI [281]. Implementing a Quality by Design (QbD) framework is crucial for robust manufacturing. QbD involves proactively defining the target product profile, identifying CQAs (e.g., size, EE, drug release), understanding the impact of material attributes and CPPs through risk assessment and design of experiments (DoE), and establishing a design space to ensure consistent quality [282]. This systematic approach, applied to processes like wet media milling or high-pressure homogenization, enhances process understanding, reduces batch failures, and facilitates regulatory approval [283].

Finally, exploring novel carrier materials and formulations with inherently improved stability profiles can mitigate manufacturing challenges. Hybrid lipid-polymer nanoparticles and nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) offer enhanced stability and drug loading capacities compared to some pure polymeric systems [284]. Advances in stabilizer chemistry, such as optimized PEGylation or alternative stealth coatings, contribute to colloidal stability during manufacturing and storage [285]. Furthermore, optimizing formulations for specific storage conditions (e.g., lyophilization with suitable cryoprotectants for long-term stability) is essential for product shelf-life and distribution logistics [275]. Overcoming the intertwined challenges of batch variability and GMP compliance demands a multidisciplinary approach, combining advanced manufacturing technologies (microfluidics, continuous processing), rigorous quality management systems (QbD), and innovative material science to pave the way for the successful clinical translation of efficacious curcumin nanotherapies.

sec.title: Regulatory and safety considerations
sec.p: The clinical translation of smart nanoparticle delivery systems for curcumin faces significant regulatory and safety hurdles, particularly concerning immunogenicity and long-term toxicity, which must be comprehensively addressed to ensure therapeutic efficacy and patient safety. Immunogenicity remains a critical challenge, as polyethylene glycol (PEG)-coated nanoparticles—commonly used to enhance circulation time—can provoke anti-PEG immune responses. Recent studies indicate that approximately 40% of patients develop anti-PEG antibodies after exposure to PEGylated nanocarriers, with pre-existing antibodies detected in 25–44% of healthy individuals due to widespread environmental exposure to PEG in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and processed foods [286]. These antibodies, predominantly IgM and IgG, trigger accelerated blood clearance (ABC) of subsequent doses, reduce bioavailability, and may cause hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis [287]. For instance, mRNA-1273 COVID-19 vaccines boosted anti-PEG IgM by 68.5-fold and IgG by 13.1-fold in clinical trials, correlating with increased hypersensitivity incidents [288]. This immunogenicity compromises curcumin delivery by reducing tumor accumulation and undermining dose-dependent anticancer effects [288, 289].

Long-term toxicity concerns center on nanoparticle accumulation in the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), particularly the liver and spleen, where reticuloendothelial clearance leads to persistent retention. Preclinical studies show that intravenously administered curcumin-loaded solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) accumulate >50% in the liver and spleen within 24 h, with residual fluorescence detectable for weeks [290, 291]. Such accumulation risks hepatosplenic inflammation, oxidative stress, and granuloma formation, yet chronic toxicity data beyond 6 months remain scarce [292]. This gap stems from methodological limitations: conventional cell cultures cannot sustain long-term exposure assessments, while animal models inadequately predict human immune responses or organ-specific damage [293]. For example, repeated dosing in rats revealed dose-dependent inflammation in hepatic Kupffer cells, but translatability to humans is uncertain due to interspecies variations in MPS activity [294]. Without robust chronic toxicity profiles, regulatory approval is hindered, as agencies like the FDA and EMA require comprehensive biodistribution and safety data extending to at least 12 months for nanomedicines [295].

Regulatory frameworks struggle to standardize safety evaluations, as nanomedicines’ complexity—variable size, surface charge, and degradation kinetics—complicates characterization and risk assessment. The FDA’s 2022 guidance emphasizes rigorous immunotoxicity screening and organ-specific biodistribution studies, while the EMA mandates comparative benefit-risk analyses for nanosimilars [296]. However, neither agency provides definitive protocols for chronic toxicity testing, reflecting broader inconsistencies in global regulations. Japan’s PMDA and India’s 2019 guidelines lack nanomaterial-specific thresholds, and regulatory divergence often classifies similar products as drugs or devices, impeding harmonized safety standards [297, 298]. Novel assessment strategies are emerging, such as adverse outcome pathways (AOPs) integrating in silico modeling and 3D microfluidic organ chips to simulate long-term liver-spleen interactions [299, 300]. Additionally, the REFINE project’s bio-physiokinetic models aim to predict nanoparticle accumulation, though clinical validation is ongoing.

To mitigate these challenges, “safe-by-design” approaches advocate for PEG alternatives, such as poly(glycerol) or zwitterionic polymers, which show reduced immunogenicity in early trials [301]. Concurrently, improved toxicity monitoring via quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models and multi-omics profiling could address long-term risks [302]. Regulatory alignment through initiatives like the Nanomedicine Characterization Laboratory (NCL) may further standardize requirements, accelerating translation while ensuring safety.

sec.title: Emerging technologies
sec.p: The future of smart nanoparticle delivery systems for curcumin (CUR) hinges on the integration of cutting-edge technologies that synergistically enhance anticancer efficacy and bioavailability. Among the most transformative advancements is the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in nanoparticle design, which transcends traditional empirical approaches. AI-driven algorithms, particularly machine learning (ML) models, analyze vast datasets on polymer-drug interactions, physicochemical properties, and formulation parameters to predict and optimize encapsulation efficiency (EE). For instance, ML techniques such as Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Gaussian Processes have demonstrated the capability to elevate EE in poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles beyond 90%, a significant improvement over conventional methods that typically achieve ~70% EE [303]. This optimization stems from AI’s ability to identify critical factors like PLGA molecular weight, lactide-to-glycolide ratio, and surfactant concentration, thereby streamlining nanocarrier development while minimizing trial-and-error experimentation [304]. Furthermore, AI facilitates the design of nanocarriers with tailored size, surface charge, and drug-release kinetics, which are crucial for improving tumor targeting and cellular uptake [305]. The integration of AI with microfluidic chip technology further refines nanoparticle fabrication, enabling precise control over parameters such as flow rates and reagent concentrations to enhance batch consistency and scalability.

Concurrently, CRISPR-Cas9 co-delivery systems represent a paradigm shift in precision oncology. Nanoparticles co-loaded with CUR and single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) can simultaneously deliver chemotherapeutic and gene-editing payloads to disrupt oncogenic pathways. For example, sgRNAs targeting the KRAS oncogene—a driver mutation in >90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDACs)—can be encapsulated alongside CUR in polymeric or lipid-based nanovehicles [306]. Upon cellular internalization, the CRISPR-Cas9 machinery induces double-stranded breaks in KRAS, silencing its expression and synergizing with CUR’s pro-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects [307]. This combinatorial approach not only amplifies tumor cell death but also mitigates drug resistance, as evidenced by studies where peptide-based nanoparticles delivered KRAS-targeting siRNA to desmoplastic pancreatic tumors, suppressing cancer progression in vivo [308]. The precision of this strategy is enhanced by ligand-functionalized nanoparticles (e.g., CCK-B receptor-targeted systems) that navigate the dense tumor microenvironment, ensuring selective delivery to malignant cells while sparing healthy tissues.

Looking ahead, the convergence of AI-optimized nanoparticles and CRISPR-Cas9 co-delivery promises a new frontier in personalized cancer therapy. AI can predict optimal sgRNA sequences to minimize off-target effects and design nanocarriers for co-encapsulating CUR and CRISPR components with high efficiency [309]. Emerging platforms, such as gold nanoparticles or bioreducible lipid nanoparticles, further enhance this synergy by facilitating endosomal escape and intracellular release of Cas9-sgRNA ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) [310]. However, challenges persist, including ensuring the biocompatibility and long-term safety of nanomaterials, addressing potential immune responses to CRISPR components, and validating these systems in large-scale clinical trials [311]. Regulatory frameworks for AI-driven nanomedicine and CRISPR-based therapies also require refinement to accelerate translational applications. sec.title: Personalized nanomedicine
sec.p: The future of personalized nanomedicine in curcumin delivery represents a paradigm shift toward precision oncology, where genomic profiling serves as the cornerstone for ligand selection in nanoparticle design. By analyzing tumor-specific receptor expression patterns through multi-omics approaches (e.g., transcriptomics, proteomics), clinicians can identify optimal targeting ligands—such as folate for FRα-overexpressing tumors or transferrin for TfR-dominant malignancies—thereby maximizing tumor-specific uptake while minimizing off-target effects [312]. For instance, FRα is overexpressed in >80% of ovarian carcinomas and 30–50% of non-small cell lung cancers, whereas TfR shows significant upregulation in glioblastoma and metastatic tumors [313, 314]. This biomarker-driven strategy leverages advanced ligand screening technologies, including phage display and SELEX, to identify high-affinity aptamers or peptides that bind cognate receptors with nanomolar specificity [315].

Recent clinical advances underscore the translational potential of this approach. Phase I/II trials of biomarker-stratified nanotherapeutics—such as folate-targeted liposomal doxorubicin in FRα+ solid tumors and TfR-directed nanoparticles for glioblastoma—demonstrate enhanced therapeutic indices and reduced systemic toxicity compared to untargeted systems [316]. Notably, the INFORM2 NivEnt trial exemplifies how molecular profiling (e.g., WES, RNA-seq) guides patient stratification for targeted nanotherapy, achieving objective responses in 85% of biomarker-selected cohorts [317]. For curcumin specifically, genomic analysis of tumor redox environments (e.g., Nrf2/KEAP1 mutations) could inform the design of stimuli-responsive nanocarriers that release curcumin upon encountering tumor-specific oxidative stress, thereby exploiting molecular heterogeneity to boost anticancer efficacy.

Artificial intelligence further revolutionizes ligand-receptor matching through deep learning models that predict binding affinities and tumor homing efficiency. Multi-omics integration algorithms—trained on TCGA data and patient-derived organoids—can simulate curcumin pharmacokinetics in virtual patient cohorts, identifying optimal ligand-receptor pairs (e.g., folate vs. transferrin) based on individual tumor receptor stoichiometry [318]. For example, Hass et al. demonstrated that AI-driven models incorporating receptor dimerization patterns predicted ligand-dependent proliferation with 92% accuracy across breast and colorectal cancers [319]. Such computational frameworks, when coupled with real-time biosensor feedback from theranostic nanoparticles, could dynamically adjust ligand density or composition during treatment [320, 321], creating adaptive “smart” systems that evolve with the tumor’s molecular landscape.

Despite these advances, clinical implementation faces hurdles. Tumor receptor heterogeneity necessitates multi-ligand nanoparticles capable of targeting co-expressed biomarkers (e.g., FRα + EGFR), while endosomal escape barriers limit cytoplasmic curcumin delivery even after receptor-mediated uptake [322, 323]. Emerging solutions include “AND-gate” nanoparticles responsive to dual biomarkers and endosomolytic polymers that disrupt endosomal membranes upon pH activation. Moreover, scalable manufacturing of patient-specific nanocarriers requires standardized quality control protocols for ligand conjugation efficiency and batch-to-batch reproducibility—challenges being addressed through microfluidic production platforms. As biomarker validation trials (e.g., NANO-GBM) mature, the convergence of genomic profiling, AI-driven design, and modular nanocarrier systems promises to transform curcumin from a pleiotropic natural compound into a precision weapon against molecularly defined cancers [324, 325].

sec.title: Sustainability and cost-effectiveness
sec.p: The pursuit of sustainable and cost-effective strategies is paramount for the clinical translation of curcumin-loaded nanoparticle delivery systems. Plant-derived exosomes (PDEs), particularly those sourced from turmeric, represent a revolutionary approach to minimizing production costs while leveraging biocompatible nanocarriers. PDEs are natural extracellular vesicles that circumvent the need for complex synthetic processes, utilizing inherent biological machinery for nanoparticle formation [326]. Recent studies indicate that turmeric exosomes can reduce synthesis costs by approximately 70% compared to conventional liposomal or polymeric nanoparticles, primarily by eliminating expensive raw materials and energy-intensive manufacturing steps [327]. Beyond economic advantages, PDEs enhance drug stability and targeting specificity. Their lipid-protein architecture facilitates membrane fusion with cancer cells, improving curcumin’s intracellular delivery while reducing off-target toxicity [328]. However, challenges persist in standardizing isolation methods (e.g., ultracentrifugation, immunoaffinity) and scaling production without compromising vesicle integrity [329].

Complementary to PDEs, solvent-free green synthesis methods have emerged as a cornerstone for sustainable curcumin encapsulation. These approaches minimize environmental hazards by avoiding toxic organic solvents, instead employing mechanisms like anti-solvent precipitation or mechanochemical reactions to form curcumin-loaded PLGA nanoparticles (CUR-PLGA NPs) [330]. Recent optimizations have achieved encapsulation efficiencies (EE) exceeding 88%, attributed to precise control over polymer-drug interactions during nanoparticle self-assembly [331]. The absence of solvents not only reduces waste but also enhances process safety and scalability. For instance, boron-assisted imine formation in solvent-free systems enables high-yield curcuminoid synthesis with minimal purification steps, underscoring the method’s industrial viability [332]. Moreover, green-synthesized CUR-PLGA NPs demonstrate superior bioavailability; their sustained release profiles in intestinal environments enhance curcumin absorption by 5.6-fold compared to free curcumin, while PLGA’s biodegradability ensures systemic clearance without residual toxicity [333].

The environmental and economic benefits of these strategies are quantifiable through life-cycle assessments (LCAs). Solvent-free synthesis reduces energy consumption by 40–60% and cuts aquatic ecotoxicity impacts by 2–3 orders of magnitude relative to solvent-based methods [334]. For PDE production, economies of scale further diminish costs, as large-scale exosome harvesting leverages agricultural byproducts (e.g., turmeric waste), aligning with circular economy principles [335, 336]. Nevertheless, regulatory hurdles and standardization gaps—such as undefined quality controls for PDE cargo or PLGA degradation kinetics—require resolution to ensure commercial feasibility. Future frameworks must integrate Safe-by-Design (SbD) paradigms, combining risk assessment with sustainability metrics like process mass intensity (PMI) to holistically optimize nanoparticle production [337, 338].

In conclusion, the synergy between plant-derived exosomes and solvent-free green synthesis heralds a transformative era in curcumin delivery. By prioritizing renewable resources, waste reduction, and cost efficiency, these approaches address the dual imperatives of therapeutic efficacy and environmental stewardship, accelerating the transition from laboratory innovation to clinical reality.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This comprehensive review underscores the transformative potential of smart nanoparticle delivery systems in overcoming the intrinsic limitations of curcumin—a naturally derived polyphenol with compelling multimodal anticancer activity. Encapsulation within advanced nanocarriers (e.g., PLGA nanoparticles, nanostructured lipid carriers, liposomes, mesoporous silica, and biomimetic exosomes) dramatically enhances curcumin’s aqueous solubility, shields it from rapid degradation and metabolism, and extends systemic circulation. These modifications collectively elevate bioavailability to therapeutically relevant levels—achieving up to a 178-fold increase in plasma AUC in humans with specific co-grinding formulations compared to unformulated curcumin—while facilitating passive tumor accumulation via the EPR effect. Critically, “smart” designs incorporating stimuli-responsive elements (pH-, redox-, or enzyme-triggered release) and active targeting ligands (e.g., folate, transferrin, hyaluronic acid, RGD peptides) enable spatiotemporal control over drug release, significantly improving tumor-specific uptake and minimizing off-target toxicity.

The therapeutic efficacy of nanoformulated curcumin extends across diverse, treatment-resistant malignancies. In triple-negative breast cancer, hyaluronic acid-decorated liposomes suppress metastasis by 70% through dual targeting of bulk tumor cells and CD44+ cancer stem cells. For pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, gemcitabine-curcumin co-loaded nanoparticles overcome stromal barriers and chemoresistance, achieving 71% tumor reduction in preclinical models. Transferrin-conjugated systems enhance blood-brain barrier penetration in glioblastoma, elevating brain curcumin concentrations 8-fold and suppressing tumor growth by 45%. Furthermore, nano-curcumin potently reverses multidrug resistance by inhibiting P-gp efflux and downregulating survival pathways (e.g., NF-κB, STAT3), while synergizing with conventional chemo/radiotherapy to sensitize resistant cells.

Despite promising preclinical outcomes, clinical translation faces significant hurdles. Heterogeneity in the EPR effect across human tumors necessitates patient stratification strategies. Challenges in scalable, GMP-compliant manufacturing—particularly batch-to-batch variability in encapsulation efficiency (21–94% for PLGA NPs)—and long-term biocompatibility assessments (e.g., hepatosplenic accumulation, PEG immunogenicity) remain unresolved. Early-phase trials of liposomal (Lipocurc™) and polymeric (NanoCurc™) curcumin demonstrate target engagement and biological activity but underscore persistent bioavailability challenges and dose-limiting toxicities (e.g., hemolysis at 300 mg/m²). Future efforts must prioritize multifunctional “theranostic” platforms integrating real-time imaging, AI-optimized ligand selection based on tumor receptor profiling, and CRISPR-Cas9 co-delivery for gene-editing-enhanced therapy. Sustainable strategies, such as plant-derived exosomes and solvent-free synthesis, offer scalable, cost-effective alternatives.

In conclusion, smart nanodelivery systems have revolutionized curcumin from a pharmacologically challenged compound into a precision oncology agent. By harmonizing enhanced pharmacokinetics, tumor-targeted delivery, and microenvironment modulation, these innovations unlock curcumin’s full potential to suppress tumor growth, metastasis, and chemoresistance. Overcoming translational barriers through interdisciplinary collaboration and advanced manufacturing will be pivotal in harnessing this promise for clinical oncology.
